entities.name: Incentive spirometry
observations: When added to routine postoperative physiotherapy after lung resection, IS did not reduce 30-day postoperative pulmonary complications: 12.3% versus 13.0%; no differences in pneumonia, mechanical ventilation, home oxygen, length of stay, or readmission.

In thoracotomy/lung-resection patients, IS was no better than thoracic expansion exercises for FEV1 decline, pulmonary complications, secondary outcomes, or length of stay when both groups received broader respiratory care.
Across 31 randomized trials involving cardiac, thoracic, or upper-abdominal surgery, IS did not reduce pulmonary complications, mortality, or hospital length of stay.

Recent cardiac-surgery evidence found IS was not superior to standard respiratory care for clinical outcomes; PaO2 was slightly worse with IS, although some vital-capacity recovery signals favored flow-oriented IS.
Recent apparent benefits largely arose from mixed or bundled interventions, so the independent effect of IS remains uncertain.

entities.name: Thoracic surgery
observations: In adults undergoing lung resection or thoracotomy, the strongest randomized evidence does not show clinically meaningful recovery benefit from adding incentive spirometry to standard respiratory physiotherapy.

entities.name: No clinical recovery benefit
observations: For adult thoracic surgery, incentive spirometry does not consistently improve postoperative pulmonary complications, pneumonia, pulmonary function, oxygenation, length of stay, readmission, or mortality beyond standard respiratory care.
Small studies suggesting benefit generally evaluate bundled preoperative and postoperative respiratory programs, limiting attribution to incentive spirometry alone.
